html:
The Great Fergana Canal is an irrigation canal about 270 kilometres long in the Fergana Valley, in what is now Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It was dug in 1939 in just forty-five days.

Some 160,000 Uzbek and Tajik collective farm workers did the work, mostly by hand with spades and baskets. The Soviet press made it a legend of people's labour; it drew on the old local custom of hashar, when a whole community turns out to work together. The canal carries water from the rivers that form the Syr Darya across the valley, to grow cotton.

It was a model for the giant water projects that followed, such as the Karakum Canal and the irrigation of the Hungry Steppe. Together these took so much river water that the Aral Sea began to shrink from the 1960s. Fergana remains the most crowded farming region of Uzbekistan.
